newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's swaggering peso defies all odds.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's swaggering peso defies all odds.

text.p: As investors already hitched to the Mexican peso hold on for a seemingly unstoppable ride, economists are wondering whether a nasty spill will follow the fairground thrill.

So far the peso has shaken off watershed mid-term elections, fears of a rate rise in the United States and a currency crisis that is still blowing ominous-looking clouds from Asia towards Latin America.

But while Asian currencies mop up after the worst of the storm, the peso is firming against all odds. Many economists believe it is looking overvalued and say the more it strengthens, the more it will have to correct.

"Hopefully what we are talking about is a short dance number, and things will start to go the other way pretty soon," said Chip Brown, senior economist for Latin America at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter.
"I just worry about what happens when the music stops."
On Friday, the peso swaggered to a five-month high and on Tuesday opened at a still firm 7.81 pesos to the dollar.
An effective devaluation in Thailand this month wrought mayhem across regional currencies, knocked onto Eastern European exchanges and pummeled investor confidence in Brazilian and Argentine stocks.
But the peso, until last year the black sheep of emerging market currencies after its December 1994 devaluation, merely wobbled before moving to greater strength.
Economists have been scrambling to revise their year-end forecasts while wondering how long the fiesta can last.
Eduardo Estrada, currency analyst at Bancomer, said the peso's ebullience had confounded all expectations.
"The peso certainly is much stronger than we expected," he said. "What worries us is the stability -- we would like to see more direction, so we can see what is in store next year."
This year the peso has hugged a narrow trading range, not straying below the 7.76 low it touched in January or above the 8.03 high it scraped in April.
Some economists estimate it is roughly 10 percent overvalued at present and fear the longer the wait, the harder the fall when depreciation eventually comes.
"The longer it takes for the peso to break 8.0 to the dollar, the more likely it is to overshoot once it finally does," said Claudio Brocado at Valores Finamex.
Short-term currency inflows amid optimism since Mexico's July 6 Congressional elections, and the positive effect of U.S. economic strength, have conspired in the peso's favor.

"The conjunction of conditions at the moment is positive -- the elections went well, inflation is low, the U.S. (economy) is good," Estrada said, adding that Mexico's current account deficit and trade balance are also in good shape.

Brown pointed to high levels of foreign direct investment (FDI) and strong portfolio flows -- in the first four months of 1997 alone FDI rose 21.8 percent over the year-ago period to more than $1.0 billion, Mexican trade ministry figures show.
The peso's stubbornness has prompted Merrill Lynch to revise its year-end outlook to 8.30 from 8.50 pesos to the dollar.
Two months ago, Bancomer also predicted the peso would end 1997 at 8.50 to the dollar. Its forecast now stands at 8.39.
A Reuter survey of 14 economists showed all of them revising their end-July peso forecasts to 7.88 to the dollar from 8.00 just two weeks ago.
"We wouldn't be surprised if it ended (the year) at 8.20," Estrada said, adding pressure would likely build in two months' time.

"Going by what has happened in other years, there will be some pressure on the peso around October or the end of September," he said, pointing to speculation on Mexico's 1998 economic plans, and uncertainty before the annual November Pacto where the government, business and labor agree wage levels.
Mexico's new lower house, formed after mid-term elections that deprived the ruling party of its long-held majority, also meets for the first time in September.
"Let's wait till they start to fight in Congress. Then we'll see the reaction," Estrada said.
